notes: Tuesday 3 Nov 2026 world issue (Taipei ~08:00). Window: Mon 2 Nov (US Election Day is Tue 3 Nov). Economy: oil falls 7% on US-Iran deal hopes; Ryanair fare rises and pay freeze; Trump drops South Africa and Rwanda from Agoa; Fed to vote less often. Tech (USA): Anthropic revised S-1 ($17bn Q3, $895bn commitments); chatbots mislead voters; Palantir commercial beats government; Intel foundry test after 45% plunge. Politics: Supreme Court rules against Trump on California ballots; six things to watch on election night; Russian bombs kill 26 at Ukraine aid centre; Burnham slavery apology dialogue. Literature (USA): Readwise e-bookstore (hot); Clint Smith on WWII (hot); LitHub November nonfiction and SFF picks (hot). Social: Australia under-16 social media ban in High Court; UK softens care-worker settlement plan; first US bird flu death this year; DV survivor and late tagging. Sources: CNBC, BBC, The Guardian, NPR, Publishers Weekly, Literary Hub.

stories.headline: Oil prices drop more than 7% as the US and Iran both talk about a deal
stories.dek: US crude fell to about $96 a barrel, its biggest one-day drop since July. But traders have seen 'peace hopes' come and go before.
stories.caveman: For eight months, fighting involving Iran has scared energy markets, because a lot of the world's oil passes near Iran. On Monday, both sides sounded softer. President Trump told reporters Iran wants to 'make a deal and that could happen.' Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Trump would rather solve this peacefully, though he 'hasn't made a decision' about new strikes. Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said Tehran wants to fix problems through talks, and its foreign minister said a deal is possible if Washington shows 'goodwill.' Result: US oil (WTI) fell 7.4% to $96.46 a barrel and global Brent oil fell 7.6% to $104.77. Prices had jumped more than 10% in October because traders feared a bigger war after the US midterm elections. CNBC notes this has happened before: prices fell on peace rumors, then the fighting got worse and prices shot back up.
stories.why_it_matters: Oil prices flow into almost everything: gas, plane tickets, food delivery, factory costs. A real deal could cool inflation around the world, including in Taiwan.
stories.camps: Optimists say both governments now have reasons to make a deal, and markets are right to relax. Skeptics say talk is cheap: past 'peace hopes' collapsed, and oil is still far above normal. Some critics also note the timing, one day before US elections, and say voters should watch actions, not words.
stories.image_alt: Crude oil storage tanks seen from above

terms.explain: The standard unit for oil: about 159 liters.
West Texas Intermediate, the main price for US crude oil.
The main international oil price, based on oil from the North Sea.
Raw oil pumped from the ground before it is turned into gasoline or jet fuel.
US elections held halfway through a president's four-year term, for Congress and many state jobs.

stories.headline: Ryanair warns of 'double-digit' fare rises next summer and may freeze staff pay
stories.dek: Europe's biggest budget airline says its fuel bill could jump by €2 billion because of the war with Iran. Its profit fell 16%.
stories.caveman: Ryanair is a low-cost airline that flies all over Europe. On Monday it said plane tickets next summer will be 'materially higher', meaning a lot more expensive, because jet fuel costs shot up after the US-Israel war with Iran. Boss Michael O'Leary said fares need to rise by 'double digits' (10% or more), maybe even 20% to fully cover fuel, though he doubts they'll get that high. Ryanair also said it is thinking about a temporary pay freeze for workers and will slow hiring. Unite, a union for Ryanair staff, said nobody had told it about any such plan. Profit before tax for April to September fell 16% to €2.4 billion. Ryanair had 'hedged' 80% of its fuel, meaning it bought it ahead at fixed prices, but the other 20% cost much more.
stories.why_it_matters: When a giant budget airline raises prices, the whole travel market usually follows. Cheap flights may get harder to find in 2027, and workers may pay part of the bill.
stories.camps: Ryanair says it has no choice: fuel is one of its biggest costs. Unions say workers should not pay for a war they did not start, especially while the company is still very profitable. Travelers' groups say airlines raise fares fast when fuel rises but cut them slowly when fuel falls.
stories.image_alt: A Ryanair plane on an airport runway

terms.explain: An airline that sells cheap basic tickets and charges extra for things like bags.
Buying fuel ahead of time at a fixed price, to protect against price jumps.
When a company stops giving raises for a period of time.
Money a company made before paying taxes.
A group of workers who join together to bargain for better pay and conditions.

stories.headline: Trump moves to kick South Africa and Rwanda out of a US-Africa trade deal
stories.dek: The program, called Agoa, lets African countries sell thousands of products to the US with no import tax. Both countries would lose it from January 2027.
stories.caveman: Agoa (the African Growth and Opportunity Act) is a US program that lets eligible African countries send thousands of goods to America duty-free, meaning without import taxes. President Trump told Congress he plans to remove South Africa and Rwanda from 1 January 2027. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said a yearly review found both countries broke the program's rules. The US pointed to barriers against American business, and to national security and foreign policy concerns. For Rwanda, it also raised human rights, the rule of law, workers' rights and the lack of political freedom. Just a week earlier, the US Treasury sanctioned Rwanda's defense ministry, accusing it of sending thousands of troops to fight beside the M23 rebels in eastern DR Congo. For South Africa, the US also cited corruption. Trump has repeatedly clashed with South Africa's government, and last year falsely accused it of 'white genocide'.
stories.why_it_matters: Losing duty-free access can hurt factories and farms that export to the US, from cars to fruit, and the workers who depend on them.
stories.camps: Supporters say trade benefits should be a reward for good behavior, and Rwanda's role in DR Congo's war is serious. South Africa's defenders say the move is political punishment for its foreign policy, like its genocide case against Israel. Economists warn ordinary workers in Africa will feel the pain, not the leaders.
stories.image_alt: Donald Trump and South African President Cyril Ramaphosa at the White House

terms.explain: African Growth and Opportunity Act: a US program giving African countries tax-free access to US markets.
With no import tax added.
Penalties, like blocking money or business, used to pressure a government or group.
A rebel armed group fighting in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
The US official who leads trade talks for the president.

stories.headline: The Fed will vote on interest rates less often. That could mean a longer wait for cheaper loans
stories.dek: New Fed chair Kevin Warsh says one of the eight meetings next year will be a 'strategy' meeting with no rate vote, and two the year after.
stories.caveman: The Federal Reserve ('the Fed') is America's central bank. Its interest rate affects what people pay on credit cards, mortgages and car loans. On 28 October it kept its rate at 3.75% to 4%, because inflation is still well above its 2% goal. Chair Kevin Warsh then said the Fed will keep meeting eight times a year, but in 2027 one meeting will be a 'strategy' meeting with no rate vote and no statement. In 2028 there will be two, leaving six chances a year to change rates (plus emergency meetings). Some experts say that means borrowers could wait longer for relief when rates are high, and face more uncertainty when buying a home. Others say the bigger issue is whether banks pass on rate cuts as fast as they pass on increases. Even without a Fed hike, credit card rates are creeping up, LendingTree says, as card companies protect themselves from people falling behind on payments.
stories.why_it_matters: Fed decisions ripple around the world, including Taiwan's currency and stock market. Fewer votes could mean slower changes in global borrowing costs.
stories.camps: Supporters say fewer votes cut 'noise' and let the Fed think long-term instead of reacting to every data point. Critics say it makes the Fed slower to help families when the economy weakens. Consumer advocates focus elsewhere: lenders, not just the Fed, decide what people actually pay.
stories.image_alt: Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh speaking at a news conference

terms.explain: America's central bank, which sets key interest rates.
The extra cost of borrowing money, shown as a percent per year.
When prices go up over time, so money buys less.
A loan used to buy a home.
The basic rate banks charge their best customers; many credit cards follow it.

stories.headline: Anthropic's IPO filing shows $17 billion in quarterly sales, a huge loss, and $895 billion promised for computing power
stories.dek: The maker of the Claude chatbot is growing incredibly fast, but growth slowed in the third quarter, and its spending commitments are enormous.
stories.caveman: Anthropic, the AI company behind the Claude chatbot, plans to sell shares on the stock market (an IPO). On Monday it updated its official filing, called an S-1, with new numbers. In July to September it made about $17 billion in revenue, more than 11 times the same period last year. But growth slowed: up 47% from the previous quarter, compared with 144% and 132% in the two quarters before. It lost $23.29 billion in that quarter; for the first nine months it lost $104 billion, though most of that is an accounting change tied to the value of its debt-like investments, not cash spent. The big eye-opener: Anthropic has signed deals to spend about $895.4 billion, almost all on computing power and data centers. It gets much of that power from Amazon, Google and SpaceX. Its S-1 lists more than 90 pages of risks. Rival OpenAI is aiming to go public in 2027.
stories.why_it_matters: A few AI companies are making promises worth hundreds of billions of dollars. If AI demand slows, those bets could shake markets, including Taiwan's chip and server makers.
stories.camps: Fans see the fastest-growing software business in history, with real paying customers. Skeptics say losses are huge, growth is slowing, and spending promises are bigger than many countries' economies. Some investors also worry about data centers getting built on time as interest rates rise.
stories.image_alt: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei walking with security staff
stories.image_credit: Photo: AFP via Getty Images, via CNBC

terms.explain: Initial public offering: when a private company first sells shares to the public.
The official document a company files with US regulators before an IPO.
All the money a company takes in from sales, before costs.
When a company's costs are bigger than its income.
The computer power needed to train and run AI models.
A newer company that rents out AI computing power, competing with Amazon, Google and Microsoft.

stories.headline: AI chatbots are giving voters wrong election info, a study finds, and Claude made the most errors on voting questions
stories.dek: About 14% of chatbot answers on how and when to vote were wrong or out of date. Some bots even listed who to vote for.
stories.caveman: More Americans are asking AI chatbots about elections. A nonprofit called Innovating for the Public Good tested seven popular tools: Google AI Mode and AI Overviews, Anthropic's Claude, Microsoft Copilot, Google Gemini, OpenAI's ChatGPT and Perplexity. In October, 13.9% of answers to voting-logistics questions (when, where, how to vote) were outdated or wrong. About 5.9% could actually make someone miss a deadline or go on the wrong day. Accuracy depended more on which chatbot than on the question. Claude and Copilot produced three-quarters of the clear errors; on voting questions Claude was wrong or outdated about one in three times, Copilot one in four, ChatGPT one in ten. In one example NPR saw, Claude gave registration deadlines for a Michigan district that were later than the real ones. A researcher called the error rates 'extremely troubling.' Microsoft said accurate election info is a priority.
stories.why_it_matters: Today, 3 November, is Election Day in the US. The safest source for voting info is still your official election office, not a chatbot.
stories.camps: Researchers say AI sounds confident even when wrong, which is dangerous for democracy. AI companies say they point users to official sources and keep improving. Some experts argue for rules requiring chatbots to avoid election advice or clearly link to official sites; others worry about free speech and want voluntary fixes.
stories.image_alt: People looking at their phones while waiting in line outside a polling place
stories.image_credit: Photo: Jon Cherry/Getty Images, via NPR

terms.explain: A computer program you can type or talk to, which answers in human-like language.
False or misleading information, shared by mistake or on purpose.
Signing up officially so you are allowed to vote.
An organization that doesn't try to make profit for owners.
The practical details: when, where and how something happens.

stories.headline: Palantir's business sales pass its government sales for the first time, as companies rush to use its AI tools
stories.dek: Revenue nearly doubled and topped $2 billion in a quarter. CEO Alex Karp again said AI labs should be nationalized.
stories.caveman: Palantir is a US data and AI software company, long known for working with the military, spy agencies and immigration enforcement. On Monday it reported July-September results that beat Wall Street's guesses. Total revenue nearly doubled from a year ago and passed $2 billion for the first time. Profit more than doubled to $1.13 billion. The big change: US business (commercial) revenue jumped 148% to $984 million, beating US government revenue of $953 million (up 96%) for the first time. Palantir raised its forecast for the year to about $8.53 billion in revenue. CEO Alex Karp said nobody in software has had results like this, ever. He again said governments should nationalize the big AI labs, calling it the 'only realistic way' to handle who is responsible when AI causes harm. The stock still dipped about 3% after hours.
stories.why_it_matters: Palantir shows AI is moving from hype into everyday company systems. Its government work also raises big questions about surveillance and privacy.
stories.camps: Investors cheer the growth and profits. Civil-liberties groups criticize Palantir's role in immigration enforcement and policing data. Some observers find it striking that a tech CEO calls for nationalizing AI labs, while others see it as a dig at rivals like OpenAI and Anthropic.
stories.image_alt: Palantir CEO Alex Karp speaking to reporters

When a government takes ownership or control of a private company.
A company's own forecast of future sales or profit.

stories.headline: Intel's stock fell 45% in October. Now its plan to make chips for other companies faces a big test
stories.dek: The PC slump and memory shortages hit Intel hard. It still has no big outside customer for its most advanced chips, the area where TSMC leads.
stories.caveman: Intel is an American chip company. For years it has tried to build a 'foundry' business: making chips for other companies, the way Taiwan's TSMC does. It has spent a lot of its $108 billion in factory spending over five years on this, but still has no major customer for its newest chips. Its stock had risen sixfold after the US government took a 10% stake in August 2025 and Nvidia invested $5 billion. Then last Thursday Intel said sales this quarter would be $1-2 billion below expectations, because people are not upgrading PCs as memory and parts get pricey. The stock fell 29% on Friday, its worst day since the 1970s, and 45% for October, its worst month on record. Its data-center chip sales grew 78%, but Intel can't make enough. It is moving some Oregon factory space away from its advanced 18A chips to older chips. A former Intel board member warned that makes it look less reliable to possible foundry customers.
stories.why_it_matters: If Intel's foundry stalls, more of the world keeps depending on TSMC in Taiwan. That brings business to Taiwan but also more pressure from the US to build chips at home.
stories.camps: Bulls say Intel's AI server chips are selling well and US government support gives it time. Bears say it keeps missing goals and can't serve outside customers if it can't even meet its own demand. Policy voices argue the US needs Intel to succeed for national security, whatever the stock price.
stories.image_alt: Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan at an Intel event

terms.explain: A factory business that makes chips designed by other companies.
Intel's most advanced chipmaking process, meant to compete with TSMC.
Part ownership of a company.
A building full of computers that run websites, cloud services and AI.
A thin round slice of silicon on which many chips are made.

stories.headline: US Supreme Court rules against Trump's push to make California set aside ballots
stories.dek: The Justice Department claimed 20,000 non-citizens were on California's voter rolls but never showed how it got the list.
stories.caveman: The night before Election Day, the US Supreme Court said no to the Trump administration. The Justice Department (DoJ) had claimed 20,000 non-citizens were on California's voter lists. In mid-October it gave Los Angeles and Sacramento election officials a USB drive with names, gave them only 48 hours to review it, and demanded they separate and not count those people's ballots until they proved citizenship. Officials refused, and lower courts sided with California. The DoJ never explained how it built the list, and election officials said it seemed to contain many mistakes. Los Angeles County's top election official said DoJ gave no evidence or method. The administration had even threatened to prosecute officials who counted ballots from ineligible voters, which experts say has no legal basis. Voting-rights groups called the whole thing a ploy to cast doubt on the midterms.
stories.why_it_matters: In the US, states run elections. This ruling protects that system and means ballots in the biggest state get counted normally.
stories.camps: The administration says it is trying to stop non-citizens from voting, which is illegal. California and voting-rights groups say non-citizen voting is extremely rare and the list looked sloppy, so the real goal was to scare voters and create distrust. Some conservatives agree with checking rolls but say it must be done carefully, with evidence and time.
stories.image_alt: Voters casting ballots at City Hall in San Francisco
stories.image_credit: Photo: Bloomberg/Getty Images, via The Guardian

terms.explain: The highest court in the United States.
The US government department in charge of federal law enforcement and lawyers.
Official lists of people registered to vote.
The paper or form you use to vote.
To set aside and keep separate.

stories.headline: US midterm Election Day: six things to watch as results come in
stories.dek: Early clues from Indiana, Kentucky and Florida; independents; young voters; and close Senate fights in Michigan and Texas.
stories.caveman: Today Americans vote for all of the House, a third of the Senate, and many governors. NPR's guide: First, watch early results. Indiana and Kentucky report first (6pm Eastern, 7am Wednesday in Taiwan). If Republican-held seats like Indiana's 5th and Kentucky's 6th are close, it could signal a Democratic wave. Second, independents: since Trump arrived, Republicans do well when they win at least 46% of them. Third, Michigan's Senate race between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers; Democrats usually need about 68% in Detroit's Wayne County to win the state. Fourth, young voters: only about 1 in 5 vote in midterms, but when Democrats win them by 20+ points, they usually do well. Fifth, Texas: Democrat James Talarico leads Ken Paxton narrowly in polls, but no Democrat has won statewide there since 1994. BBC also reports this is the most expensive midterm ever, nearly $12 billion.
stories.why_it_matters: Whoever controls Congress decides budgets, investigations and what laws Trump can pass. US policy on trade, tariffs and Taiwan can shift with it.
stories.camps: Democrats hope anger over prices and Trump's policies brings a 'wave.' Republicans say their voters will show up and polls have underestimated them before, especially in Texas. Neutral analysts warn early results can mislead, because mail ballots in some states are counted later.
stories.image_alt: People walk past a voting sign in Detroit, Michigan
stories.image_credit: Photo: Spencer Platt/Getty Images, via NPR

terms.explain: The US House of Representatives, the larger chamber of Congress.
The smaller chamber of Congress, with two senators per state.
Voters not registered with either major party.
How many eligible people actually vote.
When one party wins many seats at once.
When a seat changes from one party to the other.

stories.headline: Russian bombs kill 26 at a Ukrainian village aid centre, Kyiv says
stories.dek: Huge 3,000kg bombs hit a school used to hand out aid in Komyshuvakha, then a second strike hit where people sheltered. Rescuers were among the dead.
stories.caveman: In the village of Komyshuvakha, in southern Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region, at least nine 3,000kg aerial bombs hit on Monday, the regional head said. President Volodymyr Zelensky said the first strike hit a school used for humanitarian aid, and a second hit the place where people were sheltering. At least 26 people died, including two rescuers and four police officers, according to Ukrainian officials; people were still under the rubble. Rescue work had to stop several times because of Russian drones. Russia's military did not comment. Zelensky said Russia must have known residents got aid there every week, and called it proof Russia doesn't want to calm the war. He noted that just before, Russia and Ukraine had worked together to evacuate civilians from the occupied town of Oleshky during a short ceasefire brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump. Peace talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US are due to resume soon.
stories.why_it_matters: Attacks on aid sites hurt the people with the least: elderly and poor villagers who stayed. They also make upcoming peace talks harder.
stories.camps: Ukraine says this shows Russia is not serious about peace. Russia usually says it targets military sites, but has not commented here. Many international law experts say hitting a place where civilians get aid, especially with a second strike on rescuers, could be a war crime and should be investigated.
stories.image_alt: A burned-out vehicle and damaged buildings after the bombing

terms.explain: Help like food, water and medicine given to people in a crisis.
A bomb dropped from a plane.
An agreement to stop fighting for a time.
Controlled by an enemy army.
A serious breaking of the laws of war, like deliberately attacking civilians.

stories.headline: UK prime minister Andy Burnham will ask countries hurt by Britain's role in slavery to help shape a formal apology
stories.dek: He is starting a 'structured dialogue' at the Commonwealth summit in Antigua. Downing Street rules out paying reparations.
stories.caveman: Britain played a huge role in the transatlantic slave trade, which forced millions of Africans to work as enslaved people, mainly in the Caribbean and Americas. Prime Minister Andy Burnham is heading to the Commonwealth leaders' summit in Antigua and Barbuda, which starts Tuesday. His office said he will launch a 'structured dialogue' asking affected countries what form an official apology should take, saying their input is essential. UK officials say other Commonwealth countries reacted positively. But Downing Street has ruled out reparations, meaning payments to make up for the harm. Instead, Burnham is expected to propose a system to restructure debt for countries facing high borrowing costs. Burnham wrote in the Guardian that Britain should 'show leadership again'. King Charles is also in Antigua; No 10 denied the king had been embarrassed by the plan.
stories.why_it_matters: Many Caribbean countries say slavery's harm still shapes their poverty and debt today. How Britain apologizes could become a model for other former colonial powers.
stories.camps: Supporters say an apology is long overdue, and asking affected nations first is respectful. Many Caribbean leaders say an apology without reparations is not enough. Critics in Britain say today's people shouldn't apologize for things done centuries ago, or worry it will lead to big payment demands.
stories.image_alt: Prime Minister Andy Burnham
stories.image_credit: Photo: Russell Cheyne/Reuters, via The Guardian

terms.explain: A group of 56 countries, most once part of the British Empire.
Payments or other help to make up for a past wrong.
The forced shipping of millions of Africans across the Atlantic, from the 1500s to the 1800s.
The UK prime minister's office and home; also called No 10.
Changing loan terms so a country can afford to pay.

stories.headline: Hot: Readwise launches an e-bookstore with all Big Five publishers and a 'Strava for reading' twist
stories.dek: The small, self-funded company bought a French e-book seller just to get publisher deals. Its app tracks how deeply you read and lets friends see.
stories.caveman: Readwise is a small US company (25 staff, no outside investors) known for apps that save your Kindle highlights. Now it has opened Readwise Books, an e-bookstore plus reading app, in public beta. It sells titles from all five of the biggest US publishers. Getting those deals is hard: publishers want proof you can sell e-books before they sign, which co-founder Daniel Doyon called a chicken-and-egg problem. So Readwise bought Glose, a Paris e-book seller that already had the deals. The twist: the app tracks your reading like a fitness tracker, logging words read and time, and labels stages like 'immersed' or 'active.' Friends can follow your reading sessions, like the exercise app Strava. It sent free e-readers to a couple hundred small book influencers. Sales are US-only for now. Doyon says he wants people to choose it because it's better, not because they dislike Amazon.
stories.why_it_matters: Amazon's Kindle dominates e-books. New competitors could give readers and authors more choice, but tracking reading also raises privacy questions.
stories.camps: Fans of reading challenges love the social, data-driven idea. Critics worry that turning reading into stats and public 'performance' could spoil quiet, private reading, and want clear rules on what data is collected. Industry watchers ask if any newcomer can really dent Amazon.
stories.image_alt: Screens from the Readwise Books reading app

terms.explain: An online shop that sells digital books.
The five largest US publishers: Penguin Random House, HarperCollins, Simon & Schuster, Hachette and Macmillan.
An early version of a product opened to everyone for testing.
A person with many social-media followers who can sway what they buy or read.

stories.headline: Hot: Clint Smith turns to World War II and its last witnesses in his next book
stories.dek: The award-winning author of How the Word Is Passed says teachers must reject using history as an 'ideological weapon'.
stories.caveman: Clint Smith's bestseller How the Word Is Passed looked at how places across America remember, or avoid remembering, slavery. It won the National Book Critics Circle Award. His next adult book, Just Beneath the Soil: World War II Through the Eyes of Its Last Witnesses (Knopf, May 2027), visits memorials and survivors around the world. He told Publishers Weekly the idea came while touring: people kept asking how Germany remembers the Holocaust compared with how the US remembers slavery. Visiting Germany made him realize he understood WWII less than he thought. He says these are the last years when people who lived through the war are still alive, and asks whether the weakening of the post-war world order is linked to losing those who remember how bad things can get. A former high school teacher, he will speak to English teachers (NCTE) on 21 November, urging them to teach complexity and many stories.
stories.why_it_matters: Smith's books help readers connect the past with today's fights over monuments, school curriculums and book bans.
stories.camps: Admirers say Smith models honest history: listening to people and places, not slogans. Critics of 'reckoning' history, mostly on the right, say schools focus too much on national wrongs. Smith's answer is that teaching many perspectives is not an agenda; erasing them is.
stories.image_alt: Author Clint Smith and the cover of Just Beneath the Soil

terms.explain: The Nazi genocide of six million Jews and millions of others during World War II.
A top US book prize chosen by book critics.
National Council of Teachers of English, a big US teachers' group.
Driven by a fixed set of political beliefs.

stories.headline: Hot reads: Literary Hub picks 10 nonfiction books for November, from Amazon poison hunters to the origin of 'boycott'
stories.dek: The list includes Hermione Lee, Matt O'Hara's The Flying Death and Olivia Swarthout's fun word-history guide.
stories.caveman: Literary Hub, a popular US book website, chose 10 new nonfiction books to read this month. Matt O'Hara's The Flying Death follows Richard Gill, an American who in 1938 went down the Amazon River looking for curare, the poison local tribes used on blow darts. He hoped it could cure diseases, including his own, and make him rich. Curare did change anesthesia (medicine that puts patients to sleep for surgery) worldwide, but O'Hara shows how the Indigenous people who discovered its secrets were used and left behind. Olivia Swarthout's The Wordspotter's Guide is a light, well-researched walk through English word history, like how 'boycott' came from Charles Boycott, a land agent who enforced unfair rules on Irish tenants until the community refused to deal with him. The list also includes work by famed biographer Hermione Lee, Orlando Swayne and Sarah Haas.
stories.why_it_matters: Monthly 'best of' lists help readers find books, and help smaller titles get noticed in a crowded market.
stories.camps: Readers love curated lists as a shortcut. Some critics say these lists repeat the same big-publisher books. LitHub's mix of history, science and language books shows nonfiction is broader than politics and self-help.
stories.image_alt: Covers of ten new nonfiction books for November

terms.explain: Books about real people, events and facts.
A plant-based poison used by Amazon peoples on darts; later used in medicine.
Medicine that stops pain or puts patients to sleep for surgery.
The study of where words come from.
Refusing to buy from or deal with someone as a protest.
The first peoples who lived in a place before colonizers arrived.

stories.headline: Hot: November's best sci-fi and fantasy includes 'gig-economy ghosts', queer fairy tales and a medieval abortionist
stories.dek: Literary Hub's monthly genre list says to use the extra hour from the clock change to read instead of doomscroll.
stories.caveman: Literary Hub's monthly science fiction and fantasy list mixes spy stories in space, horror and fairy tales. Curtis C. Chen's Kangaroo Forth continues his series about a secret agent who carries a pocket universe only he controls. Ry Herman's This Knight Topples Empires queers familiar fairy tales; it is based on a Romanian story, 'The Girl Who Became a Boy', following Jules on a gender-bending quest. Other picks include a far-future world with 'flicker ghosts' tied to gig work, vampire broodmothers, a present day changed by a magical role-playing game, and a medieval healer who fights for women's rights. The writer's message: curl up under a blanket and swap doomscrolling for reading.
stories.why_it_matters: Genre fiction is where many writers explore today's worries, like gig work, gender and reproductive rights, safely inside imagined worlds.
stories.camps: Fans say SFF is having a creative boom, with more queer and diverse voices. Some readers find 'issue' themes heavy-handed and want pure escapism. In the US, books with LGBTQ+ or abortion themes are also among the most targeted by school book bans, which makes lists like this matter.
stories.image_alt: Book cover art showing figures before a glowing fantasy city

terms.explain: Science fiction and fantasy.
Work done as short paid tasks, often through apps, like delivery or ride-hailing.
An umbrella word for LGBTQ+ people; 'to queer' a story is to retell it from an LGBTQ+ view.
Endlessly scrolling bad news online.
Someone who performs abortions; here, a healer in a medieval-style world.

stories.headline: Australia's ban on social media for under-16s faces its first big court test
stories.dek: A digital-rights group and Reddit say the ban takes away young people's right to communicate. The government says it won't be intimidated by big tech.
stories.caveman: Since last December, Australia has banned children under 16 from 10 platforms, including Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, Snapchat, X, Reddit and Threads. Companies must take 'reasonable steps' to keep them off or face fines up to A$99 million. Starting Tuesday, Australia's High Court holds two days of hearings on challenges to the ban. The Digital Freedom Project, led by a New South Wales lawmaker, argues the ban breaks an implied constitutional right to free political communication. Reddit is challenging too, saying the ban hurts privacy and political rights, while still obeying it for now. Two teens who started the case withdrew, but one, Noah Jones, will attend; he says money should go to removing predators and harmful content instead. No company has been fined yet, though regulators are investigating several. Meta closed about half a million accounts at the start, but many kids say they easily got around age checks.
stories.why_it_matters: Many countries, possibly including Taiwan, are watching Australia's experiment. The court result could shape how the world protects kids online.
stories.camps: Supporters, including many parents, say social media harms kids' mental health and platforms won't fix it alone. Critics say a blanket ban is too blunt, pushes teens to riskier corners, and requires age checks that collect everyone's private data. Teens themselves are divided.
stories.image_alt: Australian teen Noah Jones
stories.image_credit: Photo: Digital Freedom Project, via BBC

terms.explain: Australia's highest court, which decides constitutional cases.
A court case arguing a law breaks the country's constitution.
Checking a user's age before letting them use a service.
The Australian official who enforces online safety rules.
People's rights online, like privacy and free speech.

stories.headline: UK softens immigration plan for care workers, but many migrants will still wait 10 years to settle
stories.dek: Care workers can apply for permanent status after five years, not 15. Many others face rule changes applied to people already in the country.
stories.caveman: In the UK, 'settlement' (indefinite leave to remain) means you can live there permanently. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood had planned to make care workers, who look after elderly and disabled people, wait 15 years. After pushback from her own cabinet and health unions, she offered them a five-year route instead. But most tough rules stay: people earning under £50,000 will wait 10 years instead of five, and people who arrived irregularly, such as on small boats, could wait up to 30 years. The changes apply even to people already in the UK. Mahmood said settlement 'must be earned.' Some Labour MPs said vital workers like scientists and chefs will be caught. The Law Society said changing rules backward undermines legal certainty. The Conservatives and Reform UK's Nigel Farage called the care-worker change a 'capitulation.' No parliamentary vote is needed.
stories.why_it_matters: Many migrants, including care and health workers from Asia and Africa, built life plans around the old rules. Changing them midway affects families, jobs and trust.
stories.camps: The government says the public wants lower migration and rules that reward contribution. Unions and migrant groups say it punishes people who keep the health and care system running. The right says even the softened plan is too weak. Lawyers say changing rules retroactively is unfair whatever your view on migration.

stories.image_credit: Photo: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Shutterstock, via The Guardian

terms.explain: Permission to live in the UK permanently.
The UK minister in charge of immigration, police and security.
Someone paid to help elderly, sick or disabled people with daily life.
Applying a new rule to things that already happened or people already here.
A right-wing UK party led by Nigel Farage, focused on cutting immigration.

stories.headline: Washington state resident dies after catching bird flu from infected dairy cows
stories.dek: It is the first US bird flu death this year. Officials say risk to the public stays low, but 33 dairy herds in one county tested positive since October.
stories.caveman: Bird flu (avian influenza, H5N1) mostly infects birds, but in recent years it has spread to US dairy cows. Health officials in Yakima County, Washington, said a resident who caught it at a dairy with infected cattle was hospitalized with severe illness and died on Sunday. The person had other health problems. The Associated Press says it is the first US bird flu death this year. Since early October, 33 dairy herds in the county have tested positive. The county has three confirmed human cases; the third person, also exposed at a dairy, did not get seriously ill. Officials are contacting people who were in close contact. They stress that the risk to the general public is low; the people most at risk are dairy workers and others who spend a lot of time near infected animals.
stories.why_it_matters: Each human infection gives the virus a chance to change. Scientists watch closely for any sign it spreads between people, which could start a pandemic.
stories.camps: Public health experts urge more testing of cows and protective gear for farm workers, many of whom are immigrants and fear speaking up. Some farmers worry testing will hurt business. Experts say: don't panic, but take it seriously, and avoid raw (unpasteurized) milk.
stories.image_alt: Microscope image of H5N1 bird flu virus particles
stories.image_credit: Photo: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases/AP, via The Guardian

terms.explain: A flu virus that mainly infects birds but can spread to animals and people.

Not heat-treated to kill germs, like raw milk.

stories.headline: UK domestic violence survivor lived 'in terror' because her attacker was released from prison without a tracking tag
stories.dek: A new inspection report says nearly half of offenders aren't tagged promptly on release; some wait up to five months.
stories.caveman: Michelle, 38, lives in a mobile home with her four children. Her ex-partner punched her, threatened her with a knife and kicked in her door, and was sent back to prison more than once for breaking probation rules. When he was released again, weeks passed without an electronic tracking tag, so relatives slept on her floor to protect her. 'It is as if they are waiting for something really bad to happen,' she said. Days after The Guardian asked the government about it, he was fitted with a GPS tag and an alcohol tag; a government source said there was no link. Hundreds of survivors are asking why tags are not fitted before offenders leave prison. Instead, the private company Serco fits them afterwards. A report by the chief inspectors of probation and prisons found nearly half of offenders are not tagged promptly, and one in 10 waits up to five months.
stories.why_it_matters: Tags only protect victims if they work from day one. Gaps right after release are when survivors are often most at risk.
stories.camps: Survivors and women's groups say tag people before they walk out the door. The government says it is improving the system and denies the Guardian's question caused the fix. Critics of outsourcing say giving public safety jobs to private firms like Serco creates delays and less accountability.
stories.image_alt: Anonymous portrait of domestic violence survivor Michelle

terms.explain: Abuse by a partner or family member at home.
A device worn on the ankle that tracks where an offender goes.
Rules and supervision for an offender living outside prison.
Someone who has lived through abuse or violence.
When a government pays a private company to do a public job.
